growth_actions.instruction: Choose a reversible task with several visible flaws. Rank them by material risk, correct only the first, place the rest on tomorrow’s list, and stop at the criterion set in advance.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Record whether deferred issues caused harm, how long delivery took, and whether physical tension eased after stopping. If material risk grew, revise the risk rule instead of forcing the exercise.
growth_actions.title: Correct one material issue and defer the rest

growth_actions.instruction: Before stating a standard, ask what risk the other person sees and summarize the answer in one sentence. Then separate required correction from personal preference.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Note any information you had missed, whether the discussion reached a shared standard sooner, and whether you still expressed the boundary clearly.
growth_actions.title: Ask what risk the other person sees before stating the standard

growth_actions.instruction: Before a low-risk task, define minimum acceptance, one risk that must be controlled, and two details that may remain unfinished. Deliver when those conditions are met without raising the bar afterward.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Compare the written standard with the outcome, any rework, and whether others could use the result. Mark which feared imperfections never became consequential.
growth_actions.title: Define “good enough” for one low-risk task

growth_actions.instruction: Leave one safe, repairable imperfection untouched for twenty-four hours. Record each urge to correct it and the reason without suppressing the discomfort.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: After twenty-four hours, check the actual consequence, attention consumed, and other people’s responses. If the issue mattered, document the evidence rather than calling the exercise a failure.
growth_actions.title: Observe one acceptable outcome after choosing not to correct immediately

growth_actions.instruction: Take one recent criticism and rewrite it as an observable fact, its impact, and a bounded request. Leave room for a response without adding a moral judgment.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Keep the original and revised versions, then note whether the request could be answered, whether conflict intensity changed, and whether it addressed a material risk.
growth_actions.title: Turn one criticism into a specific request

sections.lead: If this candidate fits, attention may repeatedly return to standards, responsibility, and what could be improved.
paragraphs: When rules are vague or quality slips, you may first look for what would make the situation correct before addressing disappointment. That sequence across work, home, and private tasks is more informative than one instance of conscientiousness.

The protected need may be to act with integrity and remain accountable, rather than to be flawless. If standards relax easily in low-risk settings or tighten only under evaluation, role demands may explain the behavior better.
points: Repeatedly noticing deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps supports this candidate more than one isolated behavior.
If role accountability or a realistic need to prevent rework explains the pattern better, a stable type hypothesis deserves less weight.

sections.lead: You may notice standards, responsibility, and what could be improved earlier than people around you and allocate effort from there.
paragraphs: While others are still debating direction, you may already separate non-negotiable standards from details likely to create rework. The protected concern is often reliability and responsibility, not neatness alone.
In a low-risk task with no stated rules, voluntarily defining completion criteria supports this candidate. Doing so only under formal evaluation points more strongly to role demand.

sections.lead: The visible move may be to correct the deviation or clarify the rule before naming disappointment; the less spoken need may be to act with integrity without making flawlessness the price of self-respect.
paragraphs: Under pressure, you may check more often, correct details, tighten expectations, or become less flexible in order to restore order. That response can protect quality, but in a low-risk situation it can also narrow your options. This is an observable tendency, not a diagnosis or a confirmed defense mechanism.

Your effort to prevent errors may be heard as criticism or fault-finding. That possibility is a communication hypothesis: check what you intended, what the other person heard, and whether the risk was clear.
points: The visible move may be to check the rule and correct the problem; its purpose still requires contextual and first-person evidence.
Even when the aim is to act with integrity and dependable standards, another person’s reported impact remains independent evidence.

sections.lead: A possible habitual sequence is to spot a defect, contain irritation, tighten expectations, then scan for the next defect.
paragraphs: Possible pressure cues include missed responsibilities, confusing expectations, relaxed standards, overlooked problems, or effort that does not produce a dependable result. These are situations to observe; the report cannot determine what you fear or turn an inferred concern into psychological fact.

sections.lead: A mistyping risk is that professional rigor, role accountability, or a temporary high-stakes period can resemble this pattern.
paragraphs: You may label every correction as responsibility without separating material risk from preference or aesthetics. Ask what the correction actually protects, what evidence supports the risk, and what would happen if the detail remained imperfect.

If Type 1 doesn’t emerge as a major clue this time, think of it as a less prominent pattern: Watch to see if you’re less proactive in using standards, closures, and long-term responsibilities to calibrate your actions when rules are vague, quality drops, or responsibility boundaries are unclear. It's not a judgment that you lack a sense of principle.
points: Attention to deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps across work, relationships, and private choices carries more weight than behavior in one role.
Keep role accountability or a realistic need to prevent rework as a serious competing explanation.

sections.lead: You may show care through reliability, careful follow-through, and fixing what could cause harm.
paragraphs: Reliability, remembering details, and repairing problems may be ways you express care. In conflict, you may begin with facts, standards, and what needs to change. Add your feelings, the other person’s perspective, and the actual stakes so the discussion does not collapse into a verdict about who is right.
In a relationship with clear agreements and clear responsibilities, it may be easier for you to show that you care by being punctual, honoring your obligations, and handling problems cleanly.
points: Care may be expressed when you check the rule and correct the problem, but a type cannot specify what the other person needs.

sections.lead: A recurring relationship difficulty may be to revisit who was responsible and what would have been fair or appropriate.
paragraphs: You may be protecting quality or fairness, but if it's an issue right from the start, the other person may feel negated at first. First ask the other person if they are willing to listen to feedback, and then explain the impact of your concerns; repair in the relationship also requires the other person to be willing to respond, rather than just relying on you to make the standards clearer.

Repeated questions about rules, timing, or commitments may be an attempt to make the relationship dependable, but the immediate situation may also carry real risk. Ask which consequence matters most before interpreting the questions as criticism.

When requirements, acceptance criteria or delivery standards are still vague, it may be easier for you to break them into checklists, process nodes and review questions to help the team reduce rework.

sections.lead: In collaboration, you may value dependable handoffs and closed loops, with low tolerance for ambiguous ownership.
paragraphs: When you are quick to point out omissions, discrepancies, or inconsistencies, collaborators may first hear "being corrected" rather than hearing that you are protecting the quality of your delivery. A more negotiable approach is to first explain the risks, acceptance criteria, or common goals associated with this piece of feedback, and then distinguish between the parts that must be corrected and those that can be observed later; this is just a clue to communication friction, and it does not mean that you are necessarily picky or that others are necessarily resistant to feedback.
By explaining the risks, impacts, and shared goals before asking a question, you reduce the chance that others will interpret your warning as critical.
points: Collaboration can strain when concern with deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps is not translated into usable information and feedback.
Repair goals, ownership, and communication design before ruling out role accountability or a realistic need to prevent rework.

sections.lead: Around authority, you may over-check when leading and seek explicit standards and rationale when being led.
paragraphs: When you are in a leading, coordinating or reminding position, your influence may come from clarifying goals, standards, responsibilities and review mechanisms, so that delivery does not rely solely on personal awareness. It is suitable for use in scenarios where quality risks are high and processes are prone to drift; however, this only affects style cues and does not mean that the system determines that you have leadership capabilities or are suitable for management positions.

When others need to collaborate with you, assign tasks, or make requests, it may be easier to keep you engaged by clearly stating boundaries, priorities, acceptance criteria, and where trial and error are allowed. What is described here is a preference for collaboration. It is not a general prescription for management methods, nor does it necessarily mean that you need a high-control environment.
points: Clear authority makes it less necessary to act with integrity and dependable standards through guessing or repeated escalation.
Explicit decision rights and stopping conditions help prevent the pattern from starting to turn low-stakes preferences into principles.

sections.lead: You may remember details, initiate contact, offer practical help, and stay emotionally present.
paragraphs: Checking in, remembering details, and offering practical support may be ways you express care. Keep your capacity and your own needs visible so care remains a choice rather than an unspoken contract. In conflict, you may focus first on whether the bond has been damaged or whether your effort was seen. State the specific need or disappointment instead of waiting for the other person to infer it.

When the other person needs support or the interaction becomes cold, you may be more likely to take the initiative to approach, ask, and fill in; this shows a tendency to pay attention, but it does not mean that you must be responsible for maintaining the temperature of the relationship.

sections.lead: A recurring relationship difficulty may be to accumulate imbalance around giving, receiving, and whether effort was noticed.
paragraphs: You may express closeness with care, but unspoken needs are difficult to respond to accurately. Replace "I've done so much" in advance with "I need you to help me with something this time."

Offering help, checking on feelings, or remembering details may express care, although the person may simply hold responsibility in that moment. Name what you appreciated and ask what support is actually available instead of assuming an unlimited offer.

sections.lead: In collaboration, you may fill gaps and coordinate readily, sometimes accepting responsibilities that were never agreed.

sections.lead: Around authority, you may over-support when leading and need contribution to be seen without having boundaries ignored.

growth_actions.instruction: Reserve ten minutes each day for feelings that have not become useful output. Describe body cues, emotion, and need without converting them immediately into a plan or lesson.

growth_actions.title: Review body and relationship cost before starting the next target

growth_actions.instruction: Arrange time with someone that has no output, record, or display goal. Say explicitly that nothing needs to be achieved and keep the phone and task list out of view.

sections.lead: If this candidate fits, attention may repeatedly return to meaning, authenticity, what is missing, and the texture of personal experience.
paragraphs: You may first register whether an experience feels authentic, meaningful, and accurately yours, with particular sensitivity to what is absent or off-key. Emotional richness alone is insufficient; the question is whether difference repeatedly organizes choice.

Wanting accurate understanding is not the same as wanting to be special, and it may arise from a particular relationship or creative task. Stable engagement in ordinary, repetitive life is important counterevidence.

Nuance or emotional intensity may be heard as dissatisfaction, self-focus, or unwillingness to move on. Treat that as a possible communication gap and check what meaning you wanted to protect.

sections.lead: A mistyping risk is that creative training, grief, or a period of identity exploration can resemble this search for distinctiveness.
paragraphs: You may treat a strong feeling as proof that a situation has one meaning. Separate the feeling, the facts, and the story you are telling before deciding what action fits.

If Four doesn't emerge as a major clue this time, think of it as a less prominent pattern: Watch to see if you're less proactive in using authenticity, nuance, and unique perspective to calibrate your choices when you need to express differences, identify emotions, or illustrate personal meaning. It is not a judgment that you lack depth or have no self.

growth_actions.instruction: Each day, state your preference first in one small decision, including the option and timing, before hearing others. Do not withdraw it with “anything is fine.”

growth_actions.instruction: Place the most important task in the first available block and close one habitual activity before starting. Require only a minimum advance rather than the right overall mood.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Compare progress, reduction in routine activity, and energy. Identify the trigger that most often removes the priority from view.
growth_actions.title: Put the most important task in the first work block

growth_actions.instruction: For one delayed decision, set a date, required information, and a default option at expiry. Once information is sufficient, do not use further coordination to postpone choice.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Record whether the deadline held, the cost of delay, and unresolved disagreement. Allow only one replacement date with a written reason.
growth_actions.title: Set a firm deadline for one delayed decision

growth_actions.instruction: Before agreeing, repeat what you will own, what you will not own, and what the other person must carry. Wait for confirmation before beginning.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Check whether the commitment stayed clear, whether resentment or forgetting decreased, and whether you expanded scope merely to restore harmony.
growth_actions.title: Restate what you genuinely agree to before saying yes

growth_actions.instruction: Track the twenty-four hours after voicing one disagreement: the response, relationship change, and issue progress. Do not use immediate tension to predict permanent rupture.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Compare expected and actual consequences, keeping evidence of continued stability alongside facts that require repair or a renewed boundary.

sections.reflection_question: Review one conflict intensified by the tension between useful coordination from lowering your own priority. What was the first observable signal, and where could repair begin with facts, feelings, and a bounded request?
sections.title: How conflict escalates and how repair can begin

sections.lead: In task settings, you may tend to understand system-wide impact and pacing, contributing strongly to integration and continuity.
paragraphs: At work, your attention may go first to alignment, sustainable pace, suppressed disagreement, and whether cooperation can continue. This does not establish job fit, competence, or performance.
When multiple parties have split opinions, inconsistent rhythms, or tense relationships, it may be easier for you to keep everyone discussing at the same table.
points: The tendency to absorb disagreement, lower tension, and postpone a position can support quality or pace at the right task stage.
As the stage changes, reassess whether investment in overall stability, other viewpoints, friction cost, and familiar pace still fits.
sections.reflection_question: During a task stage when people move at conflicting speeds, friction appears, or your position may disturb the balance, how did this way of working improve quality or pace? At what later stage did it need to be complemented by a different strategy?
sections.title: How tasks move and the conditions that help

sections.lead: In collaboration, you may build consensus but need explicit personal judgment, deadlines, and non-negotiables.
paragraphs: If you wait for the situation to naturally stabilize, you may miss a critical window and the team may not know your true position. You can set a time point in advance when you must express your stance, and give a low-intensity version first: what do I prefer, what other concerns do I have, and who needs additional information.
You don’t need to explain everything at once, just express the most certain point at the moment.
points: Collaboration can strain when concern with overall stability, other viewpoints, friction cost, and familiar pace is not translated into usable information and feedback.
Repair goals, ownership, and communication design before ruling out a coordination role or a situation that truly needs de-escalation.
sections.reflection_question: In a recent collaboration friction involving useful coordination from lowering your own priority, was the missing ingredient information, feedback design, ownership, or psychological safety? What evidence shows that type need not explain it?
sections.title: Information, feedback, and friction in collaboration

sections.lead: Around authority, you may coordinate inclusively when leading and need gentle but definite priorities and follow-through when led.
paragraphs: When you're in a position of alignment, influence can come from muting the noise, embracing dissent, and allowing the rhythm to be uninterrupted by mood swings. It prompts integrated influence clues, which does not mean that you are naturally suitable for leadership, nor does it mean that team differences can only be resolved through gentleness in the long term.

When someone needs your opinion, giving the question, context, and alternative expressions in advance may make it easier for your true thoughts to emerge. It indicates a low-pressure expression of preference and does not mean that you lack a stance or can only passively cooperate.
points: Clear authority makes it less necessary to stay connected while making personal priority visible through guessing or repeated escalation.
Explicit decision rights and stopping conditions help prevent the pattern from starting to trade personal priority for immediate ease.
sections.reflection_question: In delegating, leading, or being managed when people move at conflicting speeds, friction appears, or your position may disturb the balance, which authority or stopping condition remained unclear? What observable outcome would change if it were explicit?
sections.title: Leading and being led: authority, boundaries, and interaction

sections.lead: As pressure rises, you may shift into secondary tasks, slow action, and appear agreeable while resisting internally.
paragraphs: The more an issue requires a position or a difficult choice, the easier it becomes to postpone.
Organizing, scrolling, or low-effort work takes over while the important decision remains untouched.
points: Pressure may amplify the impulse to absorb disagreement, lower tension, and postpone a position until it begins to trade personal priority for immediate ease.
Sleep, workload, and a coordination role or a situation that truly needs de-escalation must be checked alongside a type hypothesis.
sections.reflection_question: As pressure rose when people move at conflicting speeds, friction appears, or your position may disturb the balance, which action intensified first? What did it protect, when did it narrow choice, and could sleep, workload, or real risk explain it better?
sections.title: How the habit intensifies or changes under pressure

sections.lead: With more safety, you may recognize preferences sooner, decide proactively, and tolerate short-term disagreement.
paragraphs: You may bring patience and continuity to work that depends on steady maintenance rather than short bursts of novelty.
You may understand competing positions without requiring yourself to surrender your own.
points: When safety increases, the impulse to absorb disagreement, lower tension, and postpone a position is no longer the only familiar response.
Look for flexibility while attending to overall stability, other viewpoints, friction cost, and familiar pace, not evidence that you have become another type.
sections.reflection_question: When you felt safe and unhurried, did a different response appear—for example, the relationship holds after you state a disagreement? How could you tell that safety, rather than a different task, accounted for the change?
sections.title: What becomes possible when safety increases

sections.lead: Growth can mean learning to occupy space promptly while preserving connection through small, explicit choices.
paragraphs: In one small decision this week, state your preference, your reason, and what remains negotiable. If you need time, say exactly when you will return to the discussion.
Start with a low-stakes choice and practice making your position visible.
points: Growth adds an optional step before you absorb disagreement, lower tension, and postpone a position; it does not require erasing the original tendency.
Use seven days of evidence to test whether the new choice can stay connected while making personal priority visible without the familiar cost.
sections.reflection_question: The next time when people move at conflicting speeds, friction appears, or your position may disturb the balance, what small choice could you add without discarding your existing strength? What behavioral evidence after seven days would count as useful?
sections.title: Growth means adding choice, not becoming another type

sections.lead: The nine levels are a theoretical reading framework. For Type 9, The Peacemaker, they can organize observations about how overall stability, shared pace, friction, and every party’s place changes with resources and pressure, but this score cannot locate you at a level.

sections.lead: Early signals may include saying “anything is fine,” choosing low-priority tasks, or repeatedly delaying a decision.
paragraphs: Start with one low-conflict statement: name your current preference or minimum position without trying to resolve the whole disagreement.
Begin with ‘I currently prefer…’ without requiring yourself to make a final decision.

Recovery restores choice while checking whether a coordination role or a situation that truly needs de-escalation still requires practical or professional support.

entries.cost_expression: When relational responsiveness, recognition, or a sense of difference is important, feelings of self-worth may be more easily affected by external feedback; this suggests the need to view feedback and personal value separately.
entries.description: It is easier to understand oneself and others from the perspective of value, relationship position, being seen, and emotional atmosphere.
entries.observation_question: What do you care most about today, is whether things are accomplished or how you are seen?
entries.strength_expression: In scenarios where you need to take care of relationship temperature, feedback, and identity cues, this set of cues may help you notice changes in responses more quickly.
entries.stress_signal: Begin to compare excessively, care too much about relationship status, or tie emotional experience and sense of value too tightly.

entries.availability_note: This module offers theory-based observation prompts.
entries.boundary_note: Center clusters are an explanatory framework within the Enneagram theory and can only help to see where attention might land first; the current results page does not confirm your center type, anxiety level, or cognitive abilities.
entries.cost_expression: When thinking, rehearsal, or option management continues to be prolonged, real entry and commitment may be delayed; this prompts the need to set stopping conditions and reality check points.
entries.description: It is easier to process reality starting from understanding, anticipation, possibility, security and space for choice.
entries.observation_question: Is your judgment today helping you take action, or is it delaying your entry into real-life interactions?
entries.strength_expression: In scenarios where information, risks, and paths need to be sorted out, this set of clues may help you discover structures and information gaps.
entries.stress_signal: Start over-rehearsing, keep options open, delay entering the market, or replace experience with ideas.

entries.boundary_note: Stance is a theoretical grouping, not a behavioral style measure, extraversion judgment, leadership rating, or stable personality classification.
entries.cost_expression: If pushing becomes a habitual response, fatigue, limitations, loss, or relationship costs may be seen later; review should return to the specific event rather than treating it as a fixed flaw.
entries.description: In the Enneagram stance theory, the assertive group is often used to describe a tendency to push outward faster, occupy space, or pull the rhythm. It can only be used as a situational observation clue and cannot indicate that you are active, strong or outgoing in all situations.
entries.observation_question: When you take the initiative today, are you actually protecting goals, relationships, boundaries, or feelings of uncertainty? Is there a scene where you were able to stop and pace yourself as well?
entries.strength_expression: When the goal is clear, the situation is stagnant, or someone needs to take the lead, this set of clues may help you drive the pace, bear the cost of advancement, and push the next step forward; you still need to check other people's resources and true authorization.
entries.stress_signal: Observable signs of stress include faster tempo, increased intensity, harder pauses, or putting aside vulnerabilities and limitations.

entries.boundary_note: Stance is a theoretical grouping, not a compliance measure, moral evaluation, relationship diagnosis, or stable personality classification.
entries.cost_expression: If the sense of responsibility becomes a habitual reaction, "I agree" and "I should" may be mixed up, and the true needs will be expressed later; this requires calibrating the responsibility boundary with specific events.
entries.description: In Enneagram stance, the compliant group is often used to describe a tendency to act with reference to responsibilities, rules, relationship obligations, or trustworthy standards. It can only be used as a situational observation clue, but it does not mean that you are always submissive, ingratiating, or lacking in assertiveness.
entries.observation_question: When you take on something today, does it actually come from recognition, relationship responsibility, risk prediction, or fear of disappointing people? Is there a scenario where you could also clearly say no or renegotiate?
entries.strength_expression: When a promise needs to be fulfilled, a rule needs to be seen, or a relationship needs someone to take responsibility for, this set of clues may help you put responsibility into specific actions.
entries.stress_signal: Observable signs of stress include taking too much responsibility, double-checking, taking too much care of others, or having a hard time shutting down your inner “shoulds.”

entries.boundary_note: Stance is a theoretical grouping, not a measure of avoidance, an assessment of sociability, a clinical judgment, or a stable personality classification.
entries.cost_expression: If holding space becomes a habitual reaction, the action of returning to the scene may become delayed, and observation, numbness, or self-world may temporarily replace real action; this needs to be checked with specific situations.
entries.description: In Enneagram theory, the withdrawn group is often used to describe a tendency to turn inward to organize feelings, energy, understanding, or rhythm before deciding when to enter the scene. It can only be used as a situational observation clue, but it cannot mean that you are always avoiding, being cold, or lacking in action.
entries.observation_question: When you step back today, are you actually restoring energy, organizing information, protecting relationships, or avoiding conflict? Is there a scene where you were able to re-enter and take a stand as well?
entries.strength_expression: When information is overloaded, emotions need to be settled, or the pace of the scene is too fast, this set of clues may help you retain space and organize internal clues; if there is a lack of action to return to the scene, it may also be misinterpreted as exiting.
entries.stress_signal: Observable signs of stress include being quieter, more withdrawn, more procrastinating, or having difficulty bringing stance and needs back to real interactions.

entries.boundary_note: Harmonics are stress coping cues, not emotion regulation ability scores, mental health judgments, moral evaluations, or stable personality classifications.
entries.cost_expression: If de-escalation becomes an inertial response, problems may be dismissed prematurely and real losses, boundaries or conflict issues postponed; this requires going back to the specific incident for verification.
entries.description: In the Enneagram harmonic theory, the positive outlook group is often used to observe whether people tend to ease the situation, reconstruct meaning, lighten the atmosphere, or find an exit when faced with disappointment, friction, or pressure. It is not a measure of optimism, nor does it indicate that you avoid problems.
entries.observation_question: When you say "nothing" or try to lighten the mood today, are you actually restoring flexibility, protecting relationships, or letting important issues go out of sight for the time being?
entries.strength_expression: When you are under short-term pressure, the team atmosphere is sinking, or the relationship needs to be stabilized first, this set of clues may help you retain hope, reduce the sense of collapse, and gain space for subsequent processing; it is not proof of avoiding the problem.
entries.stress_signal: Observable signs of stress include rushing to turn the page, convincing yourself that it’s okay, or hiding the real costs with kindness, optimism, changing the subject, and following along.

entries.boundary_note: Harmonic is a stress response cue, not an evaluation of ability, a rating of rationality, a judgment of emotional maturity, or a classification of stable personality.
entries.cost_expression: If dealing with problems becomes a habitual reaction, emotional and relationship costs may be skipped, and human problems may be prematurely technicalized; when reviewing, you need to look at who was affected at the time.
entries.description: In the Enneagram harmonic theory, the competency group is often used to observe whether people tend to use standards, efficiency, structures, or executable steps to bring the situation back to order when faced with problems, pressure, or a sense of loss of control. It is not a measure of ability, nor does it indicate that you are always rational or apathetic.
entries.observation_question: When you turn problems into tasks today, are you actually restoring order and preventing loss of control, or are you avoiding the cost that people and relationships are suffering?
entries.strength_expression: When there is confusion, information is scattered, or responsibilities need to be implemented, this set of clues may help you organize the problem, break it down into tasks, and make the next step executable; the conclusion still needs to be tested by the situation and feedback from others.
entries.stress_signal: Observable signs of stress include cold expressions, increased speed, an overemphasis on the right thing to do, or acting like you are fixing the system rather than confronting the person who is being affected.

entries.boundary_note: Harmonic is a stress coping cue, not a mood stability diagnosis, impulsivity measure, relationship risk label, or stable personality classification.
entries.cost_expression: If a strong reaction becomes a habitual reaction, the power of expression may be seen first, but the real need, worry or injury point is covered up; this requires going back to the trigger point for review.
entries.description: In the Enneagram harmonic theory, the reactive group is often used to observe whether people tend to express tension first in situations that are unreal, unstable, unfair, or threatening. It’s not an emotional label, nor does it mean you’re always impulsive or difficult.
entries.observation_question: What is your strong reaction actually protecting today: truth, fairness, safety, boundaries, or some more sensitive point of hurt?
entries.strength_expression: When issues are suppressed, risks are downplayed, or boundaries are violated, this set of cues may help you let the cracks surface and resist pretending that nothing is wrong; the intensity of expression still needs to serve fact-checking and repair.
entries.stress_signal: Observable signs of stress include being quicker to react, quicker to defend or test others, and more difficult to distinguish between expressing a need or protecting a wound first.

entries.copy: The E105 five-point Likert form uses rating responses to form a full nine-type profile, top three candidates, a leading-candidate gap, and close-call comparison within one scoring context. It is a starting point for self-observation, and its scores are interpreted only within E105.

The FC144 two-option forced-choice form records relative preference signals across paired choices and can provide another observation after a close-call result. Both forms have the same evidence status. FC144 does not replace E105's primary candidate, top three candidates, or raw scoring facts, and its results are interpreted only within the FC144 scoring context.

E105 and FC144 use the same Enneagram interpretation framework but different response tasks, scoring sources, and error structures, so they do not share a scoring space. History, sharing, PDF, and retest surfaces retain each form's source. The page does not directly compare their values or interpret cross-form differences in the top three candidates as personality change.

Cross-form comparison is disabled. Unless a validated equivalence mapping becomes available, E105 and FC144 remain in separate scoring contexts, and history, sharing, and result-review surfaces do not infer improvement, decline, health status, or measurement precision from their differences.

This result supports personality-pattern reflection, self-observation, and dialogue. Current research does not support treating the Enneagram as a well-validated clinical scale. It is not used for mental-health judgment, treatment recommendations, hiring, job matching, competency evaluation, or individual risk assessment. Scores, leading candidates, close-call, diffuse, and response-quality states remain hypotheses to check against real situations.

A user-confirmed type records the user's own resonance after observation. It is not a system rescore or external confirmation. History and sharing surfaces present it only as a self-observation note; it does not overwrite the primary candidate, top three candidates, scorer output, or original scoring facts.

When triggered by low-quality signals, the results are still readable, but the interpretation boundaries are significantly narrowed. The page only retains light observation suggestions to avoid extending a single low-stability answer into a deterministic type of judgment; it gives priority to suggestions for retesting the same question type when the state is more stable and time is more sufficient. Switching forms can serve as another observation, but should not be used as a way to circumvent quality boundaries, find better answers, demonstrate personality changes, or compare score gains and losses.

Diffuse means the nine type signals do not yet form a clear leading pattern. The page lowers certainty about any one number and prioritizes the top three candidates, center distribution, recent counterexamples, and a seven-day observation task. Retesting provides another response sample; it does not automatically correct the result to a particular type.

A close-call means the first and second candidates are close. The page turns their differences into side-by-side comparison, counterexample checks, and seven-day observation questions without requiring a forced type decision.

entries.boundary_copy: This is a stress script observation only and does not correspond to developmental stage, medical status, or clinical judgment.
entries.example: For example: When things start to get out of control, do you want to straighten the boundaries first, find out more information, or stabilize the situation first?

entries.boundary_copy: What is observed is your interaction needs, not who is right or wrong in the relationship.
entries.example: For example: When the other person’s words make you uncomfortable, what do you want to protect first, your relationship position, dignity, security, boundaries, or your sense of calm?
entries.prompt: Choose a relationship with minor friction and record whether you would rather be understood, recognized, have boundaries respected, promised, needed, or let the situation settle down. Just write about your own needs and behaviors.

entries.boundary_copy: Blind spot only represents low resource usage, does not represent a defect, nor is it a hard judgment by the system.
entries.example: It’s not about whether you can do it, but whether it always appears a step later in a real scene. Just write a sentence of evidence.
entries.prompt: Just look at one less natural resource today: asking for help, saying no, expressing anger, relaxing and enjoying, acknowledging a need, establishing rules, showing initiative, stopping to feel, or taking on conflict.
entries.title: Day 6｜Look at a low-usage resource

entries.boundary_copy: Day7 resonance feedback only records your self-observation evidence and does not trigger a re-judgment by the system, nor will the result be silently rewritten into a new primary type.

core_motivation_difference.1: When a teammate has missed a commitment and also needs support, Type 1, The Reformer is more likely to organize action around standards, responsibility, and correctable gaps in order to act with integrity without making flawlessness the price of self-respect. This side gains support when the first adjustment concerns standards, boundaries, or ownership.
core_motivation_difference.2: Facing the same case where a teammate has missed a commitment and also needs support, Type 2, The Helper is more likely to organize action around other people’s needs, relational warmth, and response cues in order to have care recognized while naming needs directly. This side is more informative when the first adjustment concerns the resources or relationships attached to that focus.

fear_difference.1: When a teammate has missed a commitment and also needs support, concern for Type 1, The Reformer tends to rise as standards, responsibility, and correctable gaps becomes less controllable. A counterexample is sustained concern about other people’s needs, relational warmth, and response cues even after the first condition improves.
fear_difference.2: Under the same conditions, Type 2, The Helper is more likely to become uneasy when other people’s needs, relational warmth, and response cues is threatened. If restoring that condition leaves attention fixed on standards, responsibility, and correctable gaps, keep the other candidate open.

relationship_difference.1: In a relationship where a teammate has missed a commitment and also needs support, Type 1, The Reformer may show care through reliability, reminders, and repair. When the response disappoints, the first concern often still involves standards, responsibility, and correctable gaps.
relationship_difference.2: In that same situation, Type 2, The Helper may instead show care through proactive support, presence, and remembered details. Compared with Type 1, The Reformer, check whether a missing response first registers as neglect of other people’s needs, relational warmth, and response cues.

entries.resonance_feedback_prompt: Mark only observations supported by an event record or another person’s feedback. Familiarity, preference, and a single behavior cannot decide between Type 1, The Reformer and Type 2, The Helper.
entries.seven_day_observation_question: For seven days, record three events resembling “a teammate has missed a commitment and also needs support.” Did the first cue, first action, and later cost fit standards, responsibility, and correctable gaps or other people’s needs, relational warmth, and response cues more closely? Keep one event that neither candidate explains well.
entries.shared_surface_similarity: When a teammate has missed a commitment and also needs support, Type 1, The Reformer and Type 2, The Helper may both look invested, alert, or willing to take responsibility. The useful distinction is whether attention first moves toward standards, responsibility, and correctable gaps or other people’s needs, relational warmth, and response cues.
entries.short_compare_copy: Type 1, The Reformer first tracks standards, responsibility, and correctable gaps; Type 2, The Helper first tracks other people’s needs, relational warmth, and response cues. Compare the sequence in one real setting without forcing a choice.

stress_reaction_difference.1: As pressure rises while a teammate has missed a commitment and also needs support, Type 1, The Reformer may tighten standards and magnify defects. Notice whether this begins before the information is complete and what it protects in the short term.

core_motivation_difference.3: When many opportunities are available but the team can commit to only one, Type 3, The Achiever is more likely to organize action around goals, efficiency, feedback, and visible results in order to feel real and consequential without relying only on performance. This side gains support when the first adjustment concerns standards, boundaries, or ownership.
core_motivation_difference.7: Facing the same case where many opportunities are available but the team can commit to only one, Type 7, The Enthusiast is more likely to organize action around possibility, freedom, novelty, and the next option in order to retain choice while staying with what already matters. fear_difference.3: When many opportunities are available but the team can commit to only one, concern for Type 3, The Achiever tends to rise as goals, efficiency, feedback, and visible results becomes less controllable. fear_difference.7: Under the same conditions, Type 7, The Enthusiast is more likely to become uneasy when possibility, freedom, novelty, and the next option is threatened. If restoring that condition leaves attention fixed on goals, efficiency, feedback, and visible results, keep the other candidate open.

relationship_difference.7: In that same situation, Type 7, The Enthusiast may instead show care by sharing experiences, energy, and possibility. Compared with Type 3, The Achiever, check whether a missing response first registers as neglect of possibility, freedom, novelty, and the next option.

work_difference.7: At work, Type 7, The Enthusiast is likely to open options and connect opportunities before selecting a route when many options remain but the team needs one sustainable commitment. This is a sequence of attention, not a rating of competence, performance, or job fit.
work_difference.9: When many options remain but the team needs one sustainable commitment, Type 9, The Peacemaker is more likely to absorb viewpoints and stabilize pace before shaping consensus. Compare the actual first move rather than selecting the more flattering self-description.

core_motivation_difference.8: When conflict is present and direct movement competes with preserving connection, Type 8, The Challenger is more likely to organize action around power boundaries, control, fairness, and direct impact in order to remain autonomous and protective while allowing trustworthy interdependence. This side gains support when the first adjustment concerns standards, boundaries, or ownership.
core_motivation_difference.9: Facing the same case where conflict is present and direct movement competes with preserving connection, Type 9, The Peacemaker is more likely to organize action around overall stability, other viewpoints, conflict cost, and familiar rhythm in order to stay connected while giving personal priorities real weight. This side is more informative when the first adjustment concerns the resources or relationships attached to that focus.

fear_difference.8: When conflict is present and direct movement competes with preserving connection, concern for Type 8, The Challenger tends to rise as power boundaries, control, fairness, and direct impact becomes less controllable. A counterexample is sustained concern about overall stability, other viewpoints, conflict cost, and familiar rhythm even after the first condition improves.
fear_difference.9: Under the same conditions, Type 9, The Peacemaker is more likely to become uneasy when overall stability, other viewpoints, conflict cost, and familiar rhythm is threatened. If restoring that condition leaves attention fixed on power boundaries, control, fairness, and direct impact, keep the other candidate open.

relationship_difference.8: In a relationship where conflict is present and direct movement competes with preserving connection, Type 8, The Challenger may show care through protection, candor, responsibility, and steadfast presence. When the response disappoints, the first concern often still involves power boundaries, control, fairness, and direct impact.
relationship_difference.9: In that same situation, Type 9, The Peacemaker may instead show care through presence, inclusion, steadiness, and reduced friction. Compared with Type 8, The Challenger, check whether a missing response first registers as neglect of overall stability, other viewpoints, conflict cost, and familiar rhythm.

entries.resonance_feedback_prompt: Mark only observations supported by an event record or another person’s feedback. Familiarity, preference, and a single behavior cannot decide between Type 8, The Challenger and Type 9, The Peacemaker.
entries.seven_day_observation_question: For seven days, record three events resembling “conflict is present and direct movement competes with preserving connection.” Did the first cue, first action, and later cost fit power boundaries, control, fairness, and direct impact or overall stability, other viewpoints, conflict cost, and familiar rhythm more closely? Keep one event that neither candidate explains well.
entries.shared_surface_similarity: When conflict is present and direct movement competes with preserving connection, Type 8, The Challenger and Type 9, The Peacemaker may both look invested, alert, or willing to take responsibility. The useful distinction is whether attention first moves toward power boundaries, control, fairness, and direct impact or overall stability, other viewpoints, conflict cost, and familiar rhythm.
entries.short_compare_copy: Type 8, The Challenger first tracks power boundaries, control, fairness, and direct impact; Type 9, The Peacemaker first tracks overall stability, other viewpoints, conflict cost, and familiar rhythm. Compare the sequence in one real setting without forcing a choice.

stress_reaction_difference.8: As pressure rises while conflict is present and direct movement competes with preserving connection, Type 8, The Challenger may raise intensity and take control sooner. Notice whether this begins before the information is complete and what it protects in the short term.
stress_reaction_difference.9: Under pressure from a situation where conflict is present and direct movement competes with preserving connection, Type 9, The Peacemaker is more likely to delay a position and use routine activity to avoid the central disagreement. The question is whether that sequence repeats here and elsewhere, not which response is better.

fallback_template.observation_question: In the next 7 days, only specific situations, trigger points, first reactions and post-event reviews will be recorded: In key scenes, do you give priority to standards, relationship position, safety, boundaries, freedom, results, sense of reality, or overall stability? fallback_template.relationship_difference: In a relationship, how would you rather be treated: to be understood, recognized, needed, to have boundaries respected, to be committed, or to put an end to conflict first?

diffuse_sample.page_1_preview: A more reliable way to read this sample reading is to read 9, 6, and 2 together and observe how the clues of relationship, security, and tranquility appear together. The examples are deliberately left vague, reminding the reader to examine the situation, response status, and recurring behavioral cues first, rather than rushing to write a number into its final type.
diffuse_sample.short_summary: The reading sample shows how the results page weakens the single-number tone when the distribution is dispersed, and shifts the reading focus back to Top3, three centers, answer quality, and observable tasks; it is not a corrected answer for low-quality answers.

entries.average_expression: In most ordinary situations, people may fall back on familiar strategies for dealing with order, relationships, security, results, or tranquility.

entries.recovery_action: First name the most obvious observable clue at the moment, and then choose a low-risk small action for verification; this is not a treatment suggestion, nor is it used to judge whether the state is good or bad.
entries.stable_expression: When genre inertia is not amplified by high-load situations, genre cues can be used to observe expressions that are more stable and have more leeway.
entries.strained_expression: When task load, interaction tension, or insufficient recovery space are superimposed, the same set of strategies may be used harder and narrower; this is just a review reminder.

technical_note.summary: Explains forms, score spaces, interpretation boundaries, data status, and privacy handling without making diagnostic, hiring, or deterministic personality claims.
technical_note.title: Technical Note

entries.body: The FermatMind Enneagram Test provides readable and observable hypotheses about personality patterns. It presents a primary candidate, top three candidates, the full nine-type profile, and close-call comparison before returning the reader to real situations. The technical note explains how modules are derived from response signals and interpretation rules, and which content remains theoretical or provisional.
entries.title: Test target

entries.body: The E105 five-point Likert form uses rating responses to form a full nine-type profile and top three candidates. The FC144 two-option forced-choice form records relative preference signals across paired choices. Both forms have the same evidence status but different response tasks and scoring sources; FC144 does not overwrite E105's primary candidate.
entries.title: E105 and FC144 two forms

entries.body: The score for E105 is derived from Likert intensity, and the score for FC144 is derived from relative preference of pairwise choice. They are both projected into the same result shell, but do not default into the same numerical comparison semantics. This is why same model is not equal to same score space.
entries.title: Score space boundary

entries.body: Dominance Gap describes the relative gap between Top1 and Top2 in the same form and the same score space, and is used to help the system choose a conservative tone of clear, close-call or diffuse. E105 is different from the question types and scoring units of FC144. The gap cannot be used as a unified ruler across forms, groups, or time; nor is it a measurement error range, statistical confidence interval, norm ranking, external validity proof, or personality certainty.
entries.title: Dominance Gap

entries.body: The current system will output clear, close_call, diffuse, low_quality and other explanation ranges. They control the tone of the results page, the visibility of modules, and recommended actions, rather than claiming that a certain number has been absolutely proven. clear means that the explanations of the same form this time are more concentrated; close_call means that they need to be read side by side; diffuse means that the tone of a single number needs to be reduced; low_quality means that the answer signal is not enough to support strong explanations.
entries.title: Confidence Band

entries.body: When Top1 and Top2 are close, the system will not pretend to be more certain than the data, but will enter the task of pair analysis and 7-day observation. close-call is a ambiguity management bit, not a judgment modification mechanism.
entries.title: Close-call

entries.body: Diffuse refers to the simultaneous emergence of multiple type clues in the profile shape, and Top1 and adjacent candidates are not enough to support a strong primary type narrative. It is a state of reduced certainty in the scope of interpretation, not failure, ineffectiveness, confusion, or low-quality responses. The system will shift the reading focus from a single number to the Top 3 common themes, three-center distribution, evidence contrary to recent life, and repeatable observation tasks; only if these clues continue to appear in real situations are they suitable to continue to narrow the interpretation.
entries.title: Diffuse

entries.body: When a true quality signal triggers, the system enters the low_quality boundary. The function of low_quality in P0 is to narrow the tone and recommend retesting the same form, rather than labeling users unreliable.
entries.title: Low-quality

entries.body: Test-retest stability is an indicator that will be tracked in subsequent Technical Notes. P0 first discloses the definition and collection plan, and does not commit to specific stability rate figures in advance. Stability evidence needs to distinguish between retests of the same form, cross-form agreement, short-term status fluctuations, and user feedback; when the sample, time interval, and answer quality are insufficient, the page will not interpret a retest difference as a personality change.
entries.title: Retake Stability

entries.body: The agreement between E105 and FC144 is used to evaluate the overlap between the two question types on Top1 or Top3, rather than proving that the scores can be directly compared between the two. P0 first defines indicators and collection directions, and then evaluates whether to disclose specific indicators based on samples. Agreement can only show the degree of agreement between the two question types in the ranking of candidates, and cannot independently prove the external validity, clinical validity or career prediction ability of the Enneagram model.
entries.title: E105 / FC144 Agreement

entries.body: The user's Day7 resonance feedback and user_confirmed_type will be entered into the history as self-observation evidence for research and content calibration, but will not silently overwrite the primary_candidate. User feedback is an observation layer, not a re-judgment by the system; it can prompt which narratives need to be downgraded, add counterexamples, or rewrite expressions, but it cannot directly equate resonance with measurement accuracy.
entries.title: Resonance Feedback

entries.body: This test is used for understanding personality patterns and self-observation, and is not used for clinical diagnosis, recruitment screening, treatment recommendations, hard judgments on health levels, or absolute personality characterization. Wing, arrow, subtype and development stage languages ​​are only reserved as interpretation layers or future modules in the current version, and no hard judgment will be made. Technical Note's evidence levels are by default divided into: launched product rules, operational indicators being collected, planned stability indicators, and an explanation framework that is only a theoretical background; these levels cannot be mixed into the same certainty.
entries.title: method boundaries

entries.body: Public instructions only use aggregated method metrics and do not expose individual answer payloads, private observation text, or feedback records that can identify individual users. The share page does not display observation private content by default, and user_confirmed_type will not be regarded as the final type of the system. User feedback, sample content, and Technical Note indicators should all comply with the principles of minimum necessity, aggregate display, and traceability; if an indicator is still in the planned or collecting state, the page will only explain the definition and collection direction, and will not display forged numbers.
entries.title: Privacy and data
